tone_statements.citation: Crane, Thera. 2019. Totela K41. In M. Van de Velde, K. Bostoen, D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 2nd edn, 645-691. London/New York: Routledge. (HELDA self-archived reprint, hdl 10138/309934)
tone_statements.quote: Totela’s tone system can be analysed as H/Ø. An alternative analysis, proposed by Hyman (2007 for Tonga; 2016 for Totela) is a L vs. Ø system. Surface (non-intonational) tones can be H or L on short vowels, and H:, L: or HL falling on long vowels. … Nouns can have underlying H tone on any stem syllable, although surface HH is prohibited. Verbs have a lexical contrast between root H and Ø. … The most striking feature of the Totela tone system is High-tone anticipation (HTA), in which an underlying H tone surfaces on the preceding syllable.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2017. Bantu Tone Overview. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 13(1): 162-177. doi:10.5070/P7131040751 (pre-publication version of a chapter 'To appear in The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages').
tone_statements.quote: Although less common than perseverative shift, several Bantu languages have been reported where an underlying /H/ is shifted onto the preceding TBU. Thus compare Totela [K41] /o-ku-kul-a/ ® o-ku-kul-a ‘to sweep’ vs. /o-ku-kúl-a/ ® o-kú-kul-a ‘to grow’ (Crane, to appear) [...] Starting with the verb stem, most Bantu languages continue to distinguish *H vs. *L verb roots, e.g. Totela [K41] /-kul-/ ‘sweep’ vs. /-kúl-/ ‘grow’ (Crane, to appear)

tone_statements.summary: Binary privative system (H vs zero on verb roots, alternatively L vs zero); underlying H shifts one TBU leftward (anticipatory H-tone shift, o-ku-kúl-a -> o-kú-kul-a); anticipation applies within the verb + following phrase and into relative-clause subjects but not from a main verb onto its subject.

tone.says: Privative H vs toneless (surface H and L; HL fall on long vowels); nouns may bear H on any stem syllable, verb roots H vs Ø; H surfaces one syllable early (anticipation); downstep; downdrift.

sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent. Ch.2 sec.2.2.4 (pp.70-71): five vowels with contrastive length, 'although the role of length may be diminishing'; notes other Bantu Botatwe languages lack contrastive length and 'penultimate lengthening may instead be found' there; sec.2.2.5 and Appendix C (pp.369ff): tone system H(/L or zero), four surface tones H, !H, L, HL, regular high-tone anticipation, phrase-final super-low L after last H. sources.citation: Odden, David & Lee Bickmore. 2014. Melodic tone in Bantu: overview. Africana Linguistica 20: 3-13. doi:10.3406/aflin.2014.1021
sources.note: Bantu-wide survey; Totela cited from Crane 2014: melodic (grammatical) H targets stem V2 (final vowel in CV toneless stems), all negatives take the V2 melody. No Totela tone inventory given.

tone.quote: In some languages (Basaa (Makasso), Bena, Mbadja‑Kwanyama, Cilungu, Totela (Crane)), the only melodic patterns involve single tones, though they may have multiple docking and spreading patterns. ... Usually, if a tone‑mapping rule targets a non‑existent vowel, the melodic tone is mapped to the final vowel, thus the V2 H of Totela maps to the final vowel of CV toneless stems. ... negation alone is a predictor of melodic pattern in Totela, where again negation is morphologically transparent, and all negatives select the V2 melody.
tone.locator: p.6 (single-tone melodies), p.7 (V2 H on CV stems), p.9 (negation selects V2 melody)

tone.quote: Tt appears to have three tone-classes, if we ignore distinctions in vowel length, (in comparison with 2 in Pl and 4 in Sβ). ... The absence of any clear cut tone correspondences show that more investigation is needed to be done especially on Sβ and Tt to determine the exact number of tone classes. In particular the predominance of in both Sβ and Tt of a l-hl pattern suggests that tone classes have been obscured (or replaced) by some form of penultimate prominence such as reported for Cokwe and Mbunda (Guthrie 1948: 54).
